"'''Walk Like an Egyptian'''" is a song by the American [[pop rock]] band [[the Bangles]]. It was released in September 1986 as the third single from the band's second album, ''[[Different Light]]'' (1986). It was the band's first number-one single in the United States, being certified gold by the [[Recording Industry Association of America]] (RIAA), and ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'' ranked it the top song of 1987 in the US. It was also successful internationally, reaching number one in seven other countries and peaking at number three on the [[UK Singles Chart]].

"Walk Like an Egyptian" is a song by the American pop rock band the Bangles. It was released in September 1986 as the third single from the band's second album, Different Light (1986). It was the band's first number-one single in the United States, being certified gold by the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA), and Billboard ranked it the top song of 1987 in the US. It was also successful internationally, reaching number one in seven other countries and peaking at number three on the UK Singles Chart.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.wikitext:
[[Liam Sternberg]] said he was inspired to create the song while on a ferry crossing the English Channel. When the vessel hit choppy water, passengers stepped carefully and moved their arms awkwardly while struggling to maintain their balance, and that reminded Sternberg of the depiction of human figures in [[Art of ancient Egypt#Painting|ancient Egyptian tomb paintings]]. He wrote the words "Walk like an Egyptian" in a notebook. Later, Sternberg looked back in the notebook and, composing the melody with a guitar, he put together an up-tempo song with lyrics about Egyptian hieroglyphs, the Nile River, crocodiles, desert sand, bazaars and hookah pipes and then segued into modern scenes of blonde waitresses, school children and police officers.<ref>{{cite news |first=Mark J. |last=Price |title=Akron native's song 'Walk Like an Egyptian,' a smash hit for the Bangles, is still catchy after 35 years |newspaper=[[Akron Beacon Journal]] |date=September 22, 2021 |access-date=November 9, 2021 |url=https://www.beaconjournal.com/story/entertainment/2021/09/22/walk-like-an-egyptian-the-bangles-1980-s-akron-native-liam-sternberg/8414042002/}}</ref>

Sternberg referring to "the sand dance" in the song's lyrics has made some see Sternberg inspired by earlier pop culture dances associated with Ancient Egypt, such as the 1930s [[Sand dancing|sand dance]] of [[Wilson, Keppel and Betty]] and even earlier performances.<ref name="n157">{{cite web | title=MOJO Time Machine: The Bangles Walk Like An Egyptian To Number One | website=Mojo | date=2022-05-13 | url=https://www.mojo4music.com/time-machine/1980s/mojo-time-machine-the-bangles-walk-like-an-egyptian-to-number-one/ | access-date=2026-07-19}}</ref>
sections.text:
Liam Sternberg said he was inspired to create the song while on a ferry crossing the English Channel. When the vessel hit choppy water, passengers stepped carefully and moved their arms awkwardly while struggling to maintain their balance, and that reminded Sternberg of the depiction of human figures in ancient Egyptian tomb paintings. He wrote the words "Walk like an Egyptian" in a notebook. Later, Sternberg looked back in the notebook and, composing the melody with a guitar, he put together an up-tempo song with lyrics about Egyptian hieroglyphs, the Nile River, crocodiles, desert sand, bazaars and hookah pipes and then segued into modern scenes of blonde waitresses, school children and police officers.

Sternberg referring to "the sand dance" in the song's lyrics has made some see Sternberg inspired by earlier pop culture dances associated with Ancient Egypt, such as the 1930s sand dance of Wilson, Keppel and Betty and even earlier performances.

sections.heading: Recording
sections.wikitext:
Sternberg finished a demo version by January 1984 with the singer [[Marti Jones]], featuring percussion with kitchen implements. He offered it to [[Toni Basil]], who turned it down.<ref name="B2003">{{cite book|first= Fred |last= Bronson |author-link= Fred Bronson |year= 2003 |title= The Billboard Book of Number 1 Hits |edition= 5 |publisher= Random House Digital |page= 656 |isbn= 0-8230-7677-6 |url= https://books.google.com/books?id=PgGqNrqfrsoC&pg=PT665 |via=Google Books}}</ref> [[Lene Lovich]] recorded the first version of the song, but it was unreleased when she decided to take a break from music to raise her family. [[David Kahne]], who like Sternberg was affiliated with [[Peermusic|Peer International Publishing]], was the producer of ''Different Light''. He received a copy of the demo and liked it, especially Jones's "offhand quality",<ref name="B2003"/> and took the song to the Bangles, who agreed to record it.

Kahne constructed a multitrack consisting of a tape loop of him playing a "dog head shaker", overlaid himself playing a drum beat on a [[LinnDrum]] [[drum machine]] by hand, and then had each member of the group sing the lyrics to determine who would sing each verse; [[Vicki Peterson]], [[Michael Steele (musician)|Michael Steele]] and [[Susanna Hoffs]] sang lead vocals in the final version on the first, second and third verses, respectively.<ref name="SoundOnSound">{{cite magazine |last=Doyle |first=Tom |title=Classic Tracks: The Bangles 'Walk Like An Egyptian' |magazine=Sound On Sound |date=May 2021 |url=https://www.soundonsound.com/techniques/classic-tracks-bangles-walk-egyptian}}</ref> Kahne disliked Debbi Peterson's leads, so she was relegated to backing vocals, which angered her and caused tension within the group. The situation was exacerbated by the use of the LinnDrum in place of her drumming, further diminishing her role in the song.<ref>{{cite magazine|first= Gaby |last= Alter |title= Classic Tracks: The Bangles' "Walk Like an Egyptian" |date= September 1, 2009 |magazine= [[Mix (magazine)|Mix]] |access-date= February 15, 2014 |url= https://www.mixonline.com/recording/classic-tracks/classic-tracks-bangles-walk-egyptian-366116}}</ref> She plays the [[tambourine]] during their 1986 performance on BBC's ''[[The Old Grey Whistle Test]]''.<ref>{{cite AV media|title= The Old Grey Whistle Test Vol. 3 |type= DVD |publisher= BBC Video |year= 2006}}</ref> Kahne performed the [[whistling]] hook in the song that precedes Hoffs' final verse.<ref name="SoundOnSound" /> In live performances, the whistling part is either played by a keyboard and mimed by Debbi, or substituted by the band's scatting vocals.<ref>{{cite interview|first= Vicki |last= Peterson |subject-link= Vicki Peterson |interviewer= Carl Wiser |title= Vicki Peterson of the Bangles |work= Songfacts |date= November 9, 2018 |access-date= January 25, 2020 |url= https://www.songfacts.com/blog/interviews/vicki-peterson-of-the-bangles}}</ref>
sections.text:
Sternberg finished a demo version by January 1984 with the singer Marti Jones, featuring percussion with kitchen implements. He offered it to Toni Basil, who turned it down. Lene Lovich recorded the first version of the song, but it was unreleased when she decided to take a break from music to raise her family. David Kahne, who like Sternberg was affiliated with Peer International Publishing, was the producer of Different Light. He received a copy of the demo and liked it, especially Jones's "offhand quality", and took the song to the Bangles, who agreed to record it.

Kahne constructed a multitrack consisting of a tape loop of him playing a "dog head shaker", overlaid himself playing a drum beat on a LinnDrum drum machine by hand, and then had each member of the group sing the lyrics to determine who would sing each verse; Vicki Peterson, Michael Steele and Susanna Hoffs sang lead vocals in the final version on the first, second and third verses, respectively. Kahne disliked Debbi Peterson's leads, so she was relegated to backing vocals, which angered her and caused tension within the group. The situation was exacerbated by the use of the LinnDrum in place of her drumming, further diminishing her role in the song. She plays the tambourine during their 1986 performance on BBC's The Old Grey Whistle Test. Kahne performed the whistling hook in the song that precedes Hoffs' final verse. In live performances, the whistling part is either played by a keyboard and mimed by Debbi, or substituted by the band's scatting vocals.

sections.heading: Critical reception
sections.wikitext: Di Cross of ''[[Record Mirror]]'' considered "Walk Like an Egyptian" an example of the Bangles "adopting an eastern flavour amidst the statutory guitars, jangly noises, and quaint vocals, sucking in the candyfloss pop of some predictably inoffensive lyrics", which the reviewer deemed a style regression in the band's career.<ref>{{cite magazine |last=Cross |first=Di |url=https://worldradiohistory.com/UK/Record-Mirror/80s/86/Record-Mirror-1986-09-06.pdf |title=Singles reviewed by Di Cross |magazine=[[Record Mirror]] |date=September 6, 1986 |page=10 |location=London |publisher=Spotlight Publications Ltd.|via=World Radio History |issn=0144-5804 |access-date=November 6, 2023}}</ref>

sections.heading: Chart performance
sections.wikitext: "Walk Like an Egyptian" was the third single released from ''Different Light''. It debuted on the [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]] in September 1986. The song reached a peak of number three on the [[UK Singles Chart]] in November 1986 and reached number one in the US on December 20, staying at the top of the Hot 100 for four weeks, carrying it over into January 1987. The success of the song and "[[Manic Monday]]" propelled ''Different Light'' to number two on the [[Billboard 200|''Billboard'' 200]] chart, making it the group's most successful album.<ref>{{cite web|title= Bangles – Awards |website= [[AllMusic]] |access-date= February 15, 2014 |url= http://www.allmusic.com/artist/bangles-mn0000757085/awards}}</ref>
sections.text: "Walk Like an Egyptian" was the third single released from Different Light. It debuted on the Billboard Hot 100 in September 1986. The song reached a peak of number three on the UK Singles Chart in November 1986 and reached number one in the US on December 20, staying at the top of the Hot 100 for four weeks, carrying it over into January 1987. The success of the song and "Manic Monday" propelled Different Light to number two on the Billboard 200 chart, making it the group's most successful album.

sections.heading: Music video
sections.wikitext:
The music video for "Walk Like an Egyptian" was nominated for [[Best Group Video]] at the [[1987 MTV Video Music Awards]].<ref>{{cite web|title= 1987 Video Music Awards |publisher= [[MTV]] |access-date= September 1, 2009 |url= http://www.mtv.com/ontv/vma/1987/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131021052221/http://www.mtv.com/ontv/vma/1987/|archive-date=October 21, 2013 | url-status=dead}}</ref> It shows the Bangles performing the song at a concert and scenes of people dancing in poses similar to those depicted in the Ancient Egyptian reliefs that inspired Sternberg. Most of these people were filmed on the streets of New York City, although special effects were used to modify photos of [[Diana, Princess of Wales]] and [[Charles III|the then Prince Charles]], the Libyan leader [[Muammar Gaddafi]], and the [[Statue of Liberty]].

In a popular scene from the video, Susanna Hoffs was filmed in a close-up where her eyes moved from side to side. When asked about the scene in an interview, she explained that she was looking at individual audience members during the video shoot, which took place with a live audience. Looking directly at individual audience members was a technique she used to overcome stage fright and she was unaware that the camera had a close-up on her while she was using this technique, switching between one audience member on her left and one on her right.<ref>{{cite web |first= Jenny |last= Stewart |title= PlanetOut Talks to Susanna Hoffs |website= [[PlanetOut]] |date= August 8, 2009 |url= http://www.planetout.com/entertainment/2009/08/susanna-hoffs-bangles-under-covers.html |archive-date= August 12, 2009 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20090812114358/http://www.planetout.com/entertainment/2009/08/susanna-hoffs-bangles-under-covers.html}}</ref>
sections.text:
The music video for "Walk Like an Egyptian" was nominated for Best Group Video at the 1987 MTV Video Music Awards. It shows the Bangles performing the song at a concert and scenes of people dancing in poses similar to those depicted in the Ancient Egyptian reliefs that inspired Sternberg. Most of these people were filmed on the streets of New York City, although special effects were used to modify photos of Diana, Princess of Wales and the then Prince Charles, the Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi, and the Statue of Liberty.

In a popular scene from the video, Susanna Hoffs was filmed in a close-up where her eyes moved from side to side. When asked about the scene in an interview, she explained that she was looking at individual audience members during the video shoot, which took place with a live audience. Looking directly at individual audience members was a technique she used to overcome stage fright and she was unaware that the camera had a close-up on her while she was using this technique, switching between one audience member on her left and one on her right.

sections.heading: 1990 re-release
sections.wikitext: In 1990, "Walk Like an Egyptian" was reissued as a single in the UK to promote the Bangles' ''[[Greatest Hits (The Bangles album)|Greatest Hits]]'' album. It included new remixes for the song called Ozymandias Remix. It charted at number 73 in the UK.
sections.text: In 1990, "Walk Like an Egyptian" was reissued as a single in the UK to promote the Bangles' Greatest Hits album. It included new remixes for the song called Ozymandias Remix. It charted at number 73 in the UK.

sections.heading: Airplay restrictions
sections.wikitext:
"Walk Like an Egyptian" was one of the songs which were [[Clear Channel memorandum|claimed to have been banned by Clear Channel]] following the [[September 11 attacks]]. In researching this, ''[[Snopes]]'' found that the list was simply suggestions regarding songs to be sensitive about when deciding what to play.{{cite web|first= David |last= Mikkelson |title= Clear Channel Banned Songs |website= [[Snopes]] |date= March 29, 2011 |access-date= June 6, 2018 |url= https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/radio-radio/}}
- {{cite magazine|first= Heather |last= Murphy |title= It's the End of the World as Clear Channel Knows It |magazine= [[Slate (magazine)|Slate]] |date= September 17, 2001 |access-date= October 16, 2011 |url= http://www.slate.com/id/1008314/}} It was also included in a "list of records to be avoided" drawn up by the [[BBC]] during the [[Gulf War]].{{cite book|first= Mark |last= Kirby |year= 2000 |title= Sociology in Perspective |publisher= Heinemann |page= 164 |isbn= 0-435-33160-4 |url= https://books.google.com/books?id=NE7fykwlOl8C&pg=PT164}}
- {{cite news|title= Unfit for Auntie's airwaves: The artists censored by the BBC |newspaper= [[The Independent]] |date= December 14, 2007 |access-date= February 15, 2014 |url= https://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/music/features/unfit-for-aunties-airwaves-the-artists-censored-by-the-bbc-765106.html}}{{why|date=March 2022}}
